title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 56 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 416–419 (Night 56, continuing directly from nights-55), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 56 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The Bedouin brings Nuzhat al-Zamān to Damascus and tries to sell her in the slave market; a merchant haggles with him while she answers with eloquence that surprises both. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-khamsūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth and the fiftieth.
sentences.i: And when it was the fifty-sixth night,
sentences.n: The night-number is printed in the nominative throughout, as a fixed formula; it simply sets the scene, and the next unit supplies the speaker, "she said" (Shahrazād).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأنَّ الْبَدَوِيَّ لَمَّا أَعْطَى نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ الْقُرْصَ الشَّعِيرَ وَوَعَدَهَا أَنْ يَبِيعَهَا لِرَجُلٍ جَيِّدٍ مِثْلِهِ قَالَتْ لَهُ نِعْمَ مَا فَعَلْتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-badawiyya lammā aʿṭā Nuzhata al-Zamāni al-qurṣa al-shaʿīra wa-waʿadahā an yabīʿahā li-rajulin jayyidin mithlihi qālat lahu niʿma mā faʿalta
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate-one, that the Bedouin, when he gave Nuzhat al-Zamān the barley loaf and promised her that he would sell her to a good man like himself, she said to him: Excellent is what you have done.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the Bedouin gave Nuzhat al-Zamān the barley loaf and promised to sell her to a good man like himself, she said to him, "You have done well."
sentences.n: Read السَّعِيدُا^نَّ as السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ, "the fortunate, that": the print runs the two words together, and it is not the dual "the two fortunate ones". The sentence opens with "that the Bedouin, when ..." and never supplies a verb for it; the speech simply restarts at "she said to him" (the first "she said" is Shahrazād, the second Nuzhat al-Zamān). This kind of loose, run-on syntax is typical of the narrative register. نِعْمَ مَا فَعَلْتَ is the praise formula "how excellent what you did"; with no points in the print it could also be read نَعَمْ, "yes, you did", but the first reading is the idiomatic one.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا انْتَصَفَ اللَّيْلُ وَأَحْرَقَهَا الْجُوعُ أَكَلَتْ مِنَ الْقُرْصِ الشَّعِيرِ يَسِيرًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā intaṣafa al-laylu wa-aḥraqahā al-jūʿu akalat mina al-qurṣi al-shaʿīri yasīran
sentences.l: And when the night reached-its-middle and the hunger burned her, she ate of the barley loaf a little.
sentences.i: When the night was half gone and hunger burned within her, she ate a little of the barley loaf.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْبَدَوِيَّ أَمَرَ جَمَاعَتَهُ أَنْ يُسَافِرُوا فَحَمَلُوا الْجِمَالَ وَرَكِبَ الْبَدَوِيُّ جَمَلًا وَأَرْدَفَ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ خَلْفَهُ وَسَارُوا وَمَا زَالُوا سَائِرِينَ مُدَّةَ ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-badawiyya amara jamāʿatahu an yusāfirū fa-ḥamalū al-jimāla wa-rakiba al-badawiyyu jamalan wa-ardafa Nuzhata al-Zamāni khalfahu wa-sārū wa-mā zālū sāʾirīna muddata thalāthati ayyāmin
sentences.l: Then indeed the Bedouin commanded his company that they travel, and they loaded the camels; and the Bedouin rode a camel and caused-to-ride-behind Nuzhat al-Zamān behind him, and they went, and they did not cease being-travellers, a span of three days.
sentences.i: Then the Bedouin ordered his company to set out, and they loaded the camels. The Bedouin mounted a camel and took Nuzhat al-Zamān up behind him, and they journeyed on, and for the space of three days they did not stop travelling.
sentences.n: ثَلٰثَةِ is the print's defective spelling of ثَلَاثَةِ "three" (the long ā is not written, so it takes the dagger alif). وَمَا زَالُوا followed by a participle means "they kept on ...-ing".

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ دَخَلُوا مَدِينَةَ دِمَشْقَ وَنَزَلُوافِي خَانِ السُّلْطَانِ بِجَانِبِ بَابِ النَّائِبِ وَنُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ قَدْ تَغَيَّرَ لَوْنُهَا مِنَ الْحُزْنِ وَتَعَبِ السَّفَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda thalāthati ayyāmin dakhalū madīnata Dimashqa wa-nazalū fī khāni al-sulṭāni bi-jānibi bābi al-nāʾibi wa-Nuzhatu al-Zamāni qad taghayyara lawnuhā mina al-ḥuzni wa-taʿabi al-safari
sentences.l: So after three days they entered the city of Damascus, and they alighted in the inn of the sultan, beside the gate of the deputy; and Nuzhat al-Zamān, her colour had changed from the grief and the weariness of the journey.
sentences.i: After three days they entered the city of Damascus and put up at the Sultan's caravanserai beside the Deputy's Gate. Nuzhat al-Zamān's colour had changed with grief and the weariness of travel.
sentences.n: Read نَزَلُوافِي as نَزَلُوا فِي ("they alighted in"); the print joins the words. The النَّائِب is the sultan's deputy or governor in the city. وَنُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ قَدْ ... is a circumstantial clause ("while her colour had changed").

sentences.t: فَصَارَتْ تَبْكِي مِنْ أَجْلِ ذٰلِكَ فَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهَا الْبَدَوِيُّ وَقَالَ لَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣārat tabkī min ajli dhālika fa-aqbala ʿalayhā al-badawiyyu wa-qāla lahā
sentences.l: So she became weeping because-of that, so the Bedouin turned-toward upon her and said to her:
sentences.i: So she fell to weeping on that account, and the Bedouin came up to her and said to her,

sentences.t: يَا حَضَرِيَّةُ وَحَقِّ طُرْطُورِي إِنْ لَمْ تَتْرُكِي هٰذَا الْبُكَاءَ لَا أَبِيعُكِ إِلَّا لِيَهُودِيٍّ
sentences.tr: yā ḥaḍariyyatu wa-ḥaqqi ṭurṭūrī in lam tatrukī hādhā al-bukāʾa lā abīʿuki illā li-yahūdiyyin
sentences.l: O townswoman! And by-the-right-of my ṭurṭūr-cap, if you do not leave this weeping, I will not sell you except to a Jew.
sentences.i: "Townswoman, by my cap, if you do not stop this weeping I will sell you to none but a Jew!"
sentences.n: حَضَرِيَّة is a settled woman, a townswoman, as against the Bedouin's own desert people. The ṭarṭūr is the tall pointed cap, and swearing by it is a Bedouin oath. The threat has no fa- before the main clause (لَا أَبِيعُكِ), which the idiom allows after a conditional with a negative; read it as "I will not sell you". The narrative treats selling to a Jew as the worst fate; the text is voicing the Bedouin's prejudice, and we leave it as written.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ قَامَ وَأَخَذَ بِيَدِهَا وَأَدْخَلَهَا فِي مَكَانٍ وَتَمَشَّى إِلَى السُّوقِ وَمَرَّعَلَى التُّجَّارِ الَّذِينَ يَتَّجِرُونَ فِى الْجَوَارِي وَصَارَ يُكَلِّمُهُمْ وَيَقُولُ لَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu qāma wa-akhadha bi-yadihā wa-adkhalahā fī makānin wa-tamashshā ilā al-sūqi wa-marra ʿalā al-tujjāri alladhīna yattajirūna fī al-jawārī wa-ṣāra yukallimuhum wa-yaqūlu lahum
sentences.l: Then indeed he rose and took her by her hand and made-her-enter in a place, and walked to the market, and passed upon the merchants who trade in the slave-girls, and began speaking-with-them and saying to them:
sentences.i: Then he rose, took her by the hand, put her in a certain place, and walked off to the market. He passed by the merchants who deal in slave-girls and began to talk with them, saying,
sentences.n: Read وَمَرَّعَلَى as وَمَرَّ عَلَى ("and he passed by"); the print runs the words together. Note the verb: مَرَّ عَلَى is "pass by", as in older Arabic.

sentences.t: عِنْدِي جَارِيَةٌ أَتَيْتُ بِهَا مَعِي وَأَخُوهَا ضَعِيفٌ فَأَرْسَلْتُهُ إِلَى أَهْلِي لِبِلَادِ الْقُدْسِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يُدَاوُوهُ إِلَى أَنْ يَبْرَأَ
sentences.tr: ʿindī jāriyatun ataytu bihā maʿī wa-akhūhā ḍaʿīfun fa-arsaltuhu ilā ahlī li-bilādi al-Qudsi li-ajli an yudāwūhu ilā an yabraʾa
sentences.l: At-me a slave-girl: I brought her with me, and her brother weak, so I sent him to my people, to the land of al-Quds, for the-sake that they treat him until he recovers.
sentences.i: I have a slave-girl whom I brought with me. Her brother is ailing, so I sent him to my kinsfolk in the land of Jerusalem, that they might tend him until he recovers.
sentences.n: يُدَاوُوهُ is the subjunctive plural "that they treat him" (the final n of يُدَاوُونَ drops after أَنْ), spelled with two waws, one for the plural and one for the "him". الْقُدْس, "the Holy", is Jerusalem.

sentences.t: وَقَصْدِي أَنْ أَبِيعَهَا وَمِنْ يَوْمِ ضَعُفَ أَخُوهَا وَهِيَ تَبْكِي وَصَعُبَ عَلَيْهَا فِرَاقُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qaṣdī an abīʿahā wa-min yawmi ḍaʿufa akhūhā wa-hiya tabkī wa-ṣaʿuba ʿalayhā firāquhu
sentences.l: And my aim, that I sell her. And from the day her brother weakened, and she weeping, and parting-from-him was-hard upon her.
sentences.i: I mean to sell her. Ever since her brother fell ill she has been weeping, for parting from him weighs heavy on her.
sentences.n: مِنْ يَوْمِ ضَعُفَ is "from the day he grew weak", a time clause with a bare verb after يَوْم; وَهِيَ تَبْكِي is a circumstantial clause, "she weeping".

sentences.t: وَأُرِيدُأَنَّ الَّذِي يُحِبُّ أَنْ يَشْتَرِيَهَا مِنِّي يُلِينُ لَهَا الْكَلَامَ وَيَقُولُ لَهَا إِنَّ أَخَاكِ عِنْدِي فِى الْقُدْسِ ضَعِيفٌ وَأَنَا أُرْخِصُ لَهُ ثَمَنَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-urīdu anna alladhī yuḥibbu an yashtariyahā minnī yulīnu lahā al-kalāma wa-yaqūlu lahā inna akhāki ʿindī fī al-Qudsi ḍaʿīfun wa-anā urkhiṣu lahu thamanahā
sentences.l: And I want that the-one-who likes that he buy her from me softens for her the speech and says to her: Indeed your brother is at-me in al-Quds weak, and I cheapen for him her price.
sentences.i: And I want whoever is minded to buy her from me to speak gently to her and say to her, "Your brother lies ill with me in Jerusalem," and I will make her price low for him.
sentences.n: Read وَأُرِيدُا^َنَّ as وَأُرِيدُ أَنَّ, "and I want that ...". The print glues the two words. The verb that follows, يُلِينُ, is indicative, so the grammar is loose (Classical would use أَنْ with a subjunctive, يُلِينَ); we vocalise it as printed. The Bedouin is coaching the buyers to tell her a comforting lie about her brother. "Soften the speech" is the literal sense of يُلِينُ الْكَلَامَ.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَ لَهُ رَجُلٌ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍa lahu rajulun mina al-tujjāri
sentences.l: So there rose to him a man of the merchants
sentences.i: Then one of the merchants rose to meet him
sentences.n: The sentence is not finished here: it goes on in the next unit, so this one breaks off mid-sentence.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ كَمْ عُمْرُهَا فَقَالَ هِيَ بِكْرٌ بَالِغَةٌ ذَاتُ عَقْلٍ وَأَدَبٍ وَفِطْنَةٍ وَحُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu kam ʿumruhā fa-qāla hiya bikrun bāligha dhātu ʿaqlin wa-adabin wa-fiṭnatin wa-ḥusnin wa-jamālin
sentences.l: And he-said to-him, "How-much her-age?" And-he-said, "She a-virgin, grown, possessor-of intellect and-breeding and-shrewdness and-beauty and-loveliness."
sentences.i: And he said to him, "How old is she?" He answered, "She is a maiden grown to womanhood, endowed with wit and breeding, shrewdness, beauty and grace,
sentences.n: This unit opens mid-passage: a merchant is questioning a Bedouin about the slave-girl he is selling. The sentence runs on into the next one in the Arabic. The print has no ʾanna or pausal marking; بكر بالغة is simply 'a grown virgin', and the string of nouns after ذات is a construct chain.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ حِينَ أَرْسَلَتْ أَخَاهَا إِلَى الْقُدْسِ اِشْتَغَلَ قَلْبُهَا بِهِ وَتَغَيَّرَتْ مَحَاسِنُهَا وَانْقَلَبَتْ بِسِيمَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-min ḥīna arsalat akhāhā ilā al-Qudsi ishtaghala qalbuhā bihi wa-taghayyarat maḥāsinuhā wa-inqalabat bi-sīmatihā
sentences.l: And-from time she-sent her-brother to al-Quds, her-heart was-occupied with-him, and-her-fair-points changed, and-she-was-turned-about in-her-look.
sentences.i: and ever since she sent her brother away to Jerusalem her heart has been taken up with him: her beauty has faded and her very looks are altered."
sentences.n: سيمتها is a rare spelling; it most likely stands for سِيمَاهَا/سِيمَتُهَا, 'her mark, her look'. The sense is certain, the exact form is not, so it is vocalised by sense.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ ذٰلِكَ تَمَشَّى مَعَ الْبَدَوِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru dhālika tamashshā maʿa al-badawiyyi
sentences.l: And-when heard the-merchant that, he-walked-along with the-Bedouin,
sentences.i: When the merchant heard this, he set off walking with the Bedouin,

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ اِعْلَمْ يَاشَيْخَ الْعَرَبِ أَنِّي أَرُوحُ مَعَكَ وَأَشْتَرِي مِنْكَ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي تَمْدَحُهَا وَتَشْكُرُ فِيهَا وَفِي عَقْلِهَا وَأَدَبِهَا وَحُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا وَأُعْطِيكَ ثَمَنَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu iʿlam yā shaykha al-ʿarabi annī arūḥu maʿaka wa-ashtarī minka al-jāriyata allatī tamdaḥuhā wa-tashkuru fīhā wa-fī ʿaqlihā wa-adabihā wa-ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā wa-uʿṭīka thamanahā
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him, "Know, O-sheikh of-the-Arabs, that-I go with-you and-buy from-you the-girl whom you-praise and-commend about-her and-in her-intellect and-her-breeding and-her-beauty and-her-loveliness, and-give-you her-price,
sentences.i: And he said to him, "Know, O sheikh of the Arabs, that I will go with you and buy from you the girl whom you praise and extol, her wit, her breeding, her beauty and her grace, and I will pay you her price,
sentences.n: ياشيخ is printed as one word: read it as يَا شَيْخَ, 'O sheikh'. The verbs أروح، واشتري، واعطيك are bare imperfects in the print; they are read here as simple futures, 'I will go', 'I will buy', 'I will give', and the indicative after أنّي is the print's own Middle Arabic habit.

sentences.t: وَأَشْرِطُ عَلَيْكَ شُرُوطًا إِنْ قَبِلْتَهَا نَقَدْتُ لَكَ ثَمَنَهَا وَإِنْ لَمْ تَقْبَلْهَا رَدَدْتُهَا عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ashriṭu ʿalayka shurūṭan in qabiltahā naqadtu laka thamanahā wa-in lam taqbalhā radadtuhā ʿalayka
sentences.l: and-I-stipulate upon-you conditions: if you-accept-her I-pay to-you her-price, and-if you-do-not-accept-her I-return-her upon-you."
sentences.i: but I shall lay down conditions: if you accept her, I will count out her price to you; and if you do not accept her, I will hand her back to you."
sentences.n: This sentence continues the merchant's speech. عليك after رددتها is 'to you', returning her to the seller.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ إِنْ شِئْتَ فَاطْلَعْ بِهَا إِلَى السُّلْطَانِ وَاشْرِطْ عَلَيَّ مَا شِئْتَ مِنَ الشُّرُوطِ فَإِنَّكَ إِذَا أَوْصَلْتَهَا إِلَى الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانَ بْنِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ صَاحِبِ بَغْدَادَ وَأَرْضِ خُرَاسَانَ فَرُبَّمَا تَلِيقُ بِعَقْلِهِ يُعْطِيكَ ثَمَنَهَا وَيُكْثِرُ لَكَ الرِّبْحَ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-badawiyyu in shiʾta fa-iṭlaʿ bihā ilā al-sulṭāni wa-ishriṭ ʿalayya mā shiʾta mina al-shurūṭi fa-innaka idhā awṣaltahā ilā al-maliki Sharkāna ibni al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni ṣāḥibi Baghdāda wa-arḍi Khurāsāna fa-rubbamā talīqu bi-ʿaqlihi yuʿṭīka thamanahā wa-yukthiru laka al-ribḥa fīhā
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him the-Bedouin, "If you-wish, go-up with-her to the-sultan, and-stipulate upon-me whatever you-wish of the-conditions; for-indeed-you, when you-bring-her to the-king Sharkān son-of the-king ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān, lord-of Baghdad and-land-of Khurasan, then-perhaps she-will-suit to-his-mind, he-gives-you her-price and-increases for-you the-profit in-her."
sentences.i: The Bedouin answered, "If you wish, take her up to the Sultan and lay on me whatever conditions you like. For when you bring her to King Sharkān, son of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad and the land of Khurasan, she may well suit his mind, and he will give you her price and make your profit on her great."
sentences.n: فاطلع and واشرط are read with wasl alif (iṭlaʿ, ishriṭ), so no hamza is written. In بعقله the bi- is demanded by the verb لاق ب 'suit'. The king named here is Sharkān, ʿUmar's son. The genitive صَاحِبِ بَغْدَادَ qualifies his father ʿUmar, the lord of Baghdad.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ التَّاجِرُ وَأَنَا لِي عِنْدَهُ حَاجَةٌ وَهُوَأَنْ يَكْتُبَ لِي تَحْلِيلٌ فِى الدِّيوَانِ بِأَنْ لَايُؤْخَذُ مِنِّي مَكْسًا ثُمَّ تُكْتَبَ إِلَى وَالِدِهِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ بِالْوَصِيَّةِ عَلَيَّ فَإِنْ قَبِلَ الْجَارِيَةَ مِنِّي وَزَنْتُ لَكَ ثَمَنَهَا فِى الْحَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-tājiru wa-anā lī ʿindahu ḥājatun wa-huwa an yaktuba lī taḥlīlun fī al-dīwāni bi-an lā yuʾkhadhu minnī maksan thumma tuktaba ilā wālidihi ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni bi-al-waṣiyyati ʿalayya fa-in qabila al-jāriyata minnī wazantu laka thamanahā fī al-ḥāli
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him the-merchant, "And-I, to-me with-him a-need: and-it that he-write for-me an-exemption in the-bureau, by-that not be-taken from-me toll; then be-written to his-father ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān with-the-recommendation upon-me; and-if he-accept the-girl from-me, I-weigh-out to-you her-price at-once."
sentences.i: The merchant said, "I too have a favour to ask of him: that he write me a warrant in the Divan, that no toll be taken from me, and then that a letter be written to his father, ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, commending me. If he takes the girl from me, I will pay you her price on the spot."
sentences.n: وهوان is printed as one word: read وَهُوَ أَنْ, 'and it is that'. تحليل is printed without the alif an accusative would need, so it is pointed as a plain noun, 'a warrant of exemption'. تكتب is read as a passive, 'be written', parallel to يؤخذ; the print would also bear 'you write', which would turn the merchant's wish into an address to the sultan. The ؤ of يؤخذ is the print's own precomposed letter and is kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ قَبِلْتُ مِنْكَ هَٰذَا الشَّرْطَ وَمَشَيَا إِلَى أَنْ أَقْبَلَا عَلَى الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي فِيهِ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu qabiltu minka hādhā al-sharṭa wa-mashayā ilā an aqbalā ʿalā al-makāni alladhī fīhi Nuzhatu al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-he-said the-Bedouin, "I-accept from-you this the-condition." And-the-two-walked until the-two-came-up upon the-place which in-it Nuzhat al-Zamān;
sentences.i: "I accept that condition from you," said the Bedouin. And the two walked on till they came to the place where Nuzhat al-Zamān was.

sentences.t: وَوَقَفَ الْبَدَوِيُّ عَلَى بَابِ الْمَخْزَنِ وَنَادَاهَا يَا نَاجِيَةُ وَكَانَ سَمَّاهَا بِهَٰذَا الِاسْمِ
sentences.tr: wa-waqafa al-badawiyyu ʿalā bābi al-makhzani wa-nādāhā yā Nājiyatu wa-kāna sammāhā bi-hādhā al-ismi
sentences.l: And-he-stood, the-Bedouin, at the-door of-the-store-house and-called-her, "O Nājiya," and-he-had named-her by-this the-name.
sentences.i: The Bedouin stood at the door of the storehouse and called out, "Nājiya!" for this was the name he had given her.
sentences.n: Nājiya means 'she who escapes, the saved one'; the Bedouin has renamed his captive, and the next sentence shows she does not answer to it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْهُ بَكَتْ وَلَمْ تُجِبْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿathu bakat wa-lam tujibhu
sentences.l: And-when she-heard-it she-wept, and-not she-answered-him.
sentences.i: When she heard it she wept, and gave him no answer.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ الْبَدَوِيُّ إِلَى التَّاجِرِ وَقَالَ لَهُ هَا هِيَ قَاعِدَةٌ دُونَكَ وَإِيَّاهَا فَأَقْبِلْ عَلَيْهَا وَانْظُرْهَا وَلَاطِفْهَا مِثْلَمَا أَوْصَيْتُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata al-badawiyyu ilā al-tājiri wa-qāla lahu hā hiya qāʿidatun dūnaka wa-iyyāhā fa-aqbil ʿalayhā wa-unẓurhā wa-lāṭifhā mithlamā awṣaytuka
sentences.l: And-he-turned, the-Bedouin, to the-merchant and-said to-him, "Lo, she sitting; below-you and-her: so-come-forward to-her, and-look-at-her, and-be-gentle-with-her, like-what I-charged-you."
sentences.i: Then the Bedouin turned to the merchant and said, "There she sits. She is yours to look at: go up to her, examine her, and be gentle with her as I told you."
sentences.n: دونك واياها is the idiom 'here she is, take her', a pair of words in which دونك is an imperative-sense adverb and إياها the object. مثلما is printed as one word: read مِثْلَ مَا.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ التَّاجِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama al-tājiru
sentences.l: And-he-advanced, the-merchant
sentences.i: So the merchant stepped forward
sentences.n: The sentence is not finished here: it goes on in the next unit, so this one breaks off mid-sentence.

sentences.t: إِلَيْهَا بِخُلُقٍ حَسَنٍ فَرَآهَا بَدِيعَةً فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ لَا سِيَّمَا أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تَعْرِفُ بِلِسَانِ الْعَرَبِ
sentences.tr: ilayhā bi-khuluqin ḥasanin fa-raʾāhā badīʿatan fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli lā siyyamā annahā kānat taʿrifu bi-lisāni al-ʿarab
sentences.l: To-her with a-disposition good, and-he-saw-her wondrous in the-beauty and-the-grace, no especially that-she was she-knew with the-tongue of-the-Arabs.
sentences.i: ...to her with a pleasant manner, and he saw that she was a wonder of beauty and grace, the more so since she knew the speech of the Arabs.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-sentence: the verb that governs اليها ('to her') stood in the previous unit. خُلُق (disposition, manners) is our reading of the unpointed خلق; خَلْق (build, looks) is also possible. تعرف بلسان العرب is read as 'she knew the Arabs' tongue', that is, she could speak Arabic; the preposition بِـ after عَرَفَ is unusual, and the passive 'she was known by the Arabs' tongue' is a possible alternative.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُإِنْ كَانَتْ كَمَا وَصَفْتَ لِي فَإِنِّي أَبْلُغُ بِهَا عِنْدَ السُّلْطَانِ مَا أُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-tājiru in kānat kamā waṣafta lī fa-innī ablughu bihā ʿinda al-sulṭāni mā urīdu
sentences.l: And-he-said the-merchant: if she-was as you-described to-me, then-indeed-I I-reach by-her at the-sultan what I-want.
sentences.i: The merchant said: "If she is as you have described her to me, then through her I shall gain from the Sultan whatever I desire."
sentences.n: The edition prints التاجران as one word, 'the merchant' plus 'if' run together. Read it as al-tājiru in; it is not the dual ('the two merchants'), since only one merchant is speaking. He is addressing the Bedouin who owns the girl.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا التَّاجِرُ السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكِ يَا بُنَيَّةُ كَيْفَ حَالُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-tājiru al-salāmu ʿalayki yā bunayyatu kayfa ḥāluki
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her the-merchant: the-peace upon-you, O little-daughter, how your-state?
sentences.i: Then the merchant said to her: "Peace be upon you, my daughter. How are you?"
sentences.n: بُنَيَّة is the diminutive 'little daughter', a kindly form of address; the print marks it (damma and shadda), and we keep those marks.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ كَانَ ذَلِكَ فِى الْكِتَابِ مَسْطُورًا
sentences.tr: fa-ltafatat ilayhi wa-qālat kāna dhālika fī al-kitābi masṭūran
sentences.l: So-she-turned to-him and-she-said: that was in the-book written.
sentences.i: She turned to him and said: "That was written in the Book."
sentences.n: 'It was written in the Book' is a stock phrase for what fate had decreed (cf. the Qurʾān, 17:58); here it is the girl's bitter answer about her state.

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ فَإِذَا هُوَ رَجُلٌ مُحْتَشِمٌ وَوَجْهُهُ حَسَنٌ
sentences.tr: wa-naẓarat ilayhi fa-idhā huwa rajulun muḥtashimun wa-wajhuhu ḥasanun
sentences.l: And-she-looked at-him, and-lo he a-man dignified, and-his-face good.
sentences.i: She looked at him, and behold, he was a man of dignity, with a handsome face.
sentences.n: فَإِذَا here is the 'surprise' idiom: 'and lo, [there was]'. مُحْتَشِم is 'modest, respectable, dignified'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا أَظُنُّ أَنَّ هَذَا جَاءَ يَشْتَرِينِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat fī nafsihā aẓunnu anna hādhā jāʾa yashtarīnī
sentences.l: So-she-said in her-self: I-think that this one came he-buys-me.
sentences.i: She said to herself: "I think this man has come to buy me."
sentences.n: جَاءَ يَشْتَرِينِي, 'he came [and] buys me', strings two verbs together with no conjunction; the second is a circumstantial clause of purpose, a common Middle Arabic construction.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ إِنِ امْتَنَعْتُ مِنْهُ صِرْتُ عِنْدَ هَذَا الظَّالِمِ فَيُهْلِكُنِي مِنَ الضَّرْبِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat ini imtanaʿtu minhu ṣirtu ʿinda hādhā al-ẓālimi fa-yuhlikunī mina al-ḍarbi
sentences.l: Then she-said: if I-refused from-him, I-became with this the-oppressor, and-he-destroys-me from the-beating.
sentences.i: Then she said: "If I refuse this man, I shall remain with this brute, and he will beat me to death."
sentences.n: 'I-became' (صِرْتُ) is used for 'I shall be, I shall remain' in the answer to a conditional. فَيُهْلِكُنِي is indicative, where classical Arabic would have the subjunctive after فَـ; we vocalise what the text says.

sentences.t: فَعَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ هَذَا رَجُلٌ وَجْهُهُ حَسَنٌ وَهُوَ أَرْجَى لِي لِلْخَيْرِ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَدَوِيِّ الْجِلْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿalā kulli ḥālin hādhā rajulun wajhuhu ḥasanun wa-huwa arjā lī li-al-khayri min hādhā al-badawiyyi al-jilfi
sentences.l: So upon every state: this a-man his-face good, and-he more-hopeful for-me for-the-good than this the-Bedouin the-boorish.
sentences.i: At any rate, this is a man with a handsome face, and I may hope more from him for any good than from this boorish Bedouin.

sentences.t: وَلَعَلَّهُ مَا جَاءَ إِلَّا لِيَسْمَعَ مَنْطِقِى فَإِنِّي أُجَاوِبُهُ جَوَابًا حَسَنًا
sentences.tr: wa-laʿallahu mā jāʾa illā li-yasmaʿa manṭiqī fa-innī ujāwibuhu jawāban ḥasanan
sentences.l: And-perhaps-he not he-came except to-he-hear my-speech; so-indeed-I I-answer-him an-answer good.
sentences.i: Perhaps he has come only to hear me speak; so I shall answer him well.
sentences.n: The print spells منطقي with a final ى (alif maqsūra shape) for the ending -ī; read it manṭiqī, 'my speech'. This is a spelling habit of the edition, kept as printed.

sentences.t: كُلُّ ذَلِكَ وَعَيْنُهَا فِى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: kullu dhālika wa-ʿaynuhā fī al-arḍi
sentences.l: All that, and-her-eye on the-ground.
sentences.i: All this while her eyes were fixed on the ground.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَفَعَتْ بَصَرَهَا إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ بِكَلَامٍ عَذْبٍ وَعَلَيْكَ السَّلَامُ يَاسَيِّدِي وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ بِهَذَا أَمَرَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
sentences.tr: thumma rafaʿat baṣarahā ilayhi wa-qālat lahu bi-kalāmin ʿadhbin wa-ʿalayka al-salāmu yā sayyidī wa-raḥmatu allāhi wa-barakātuhu bi-hādhā amara al-nabiyyu ṣallā allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallama
sentences.l: Then she-raised her-sight to-him and-she-said to-him with-speech sweet: and-upon-you the-peace, O my-master, and-the-mercy of-God and-His-blessings; with-this commanded the-Prophet, God-bless-him and-grant-peace.
sentences.i: Then she raised her eyes to him and said to him in sweet speech: "And upon you be peace, my lord, and the mercy of God and His blessings. This is what the Prophet commanded, God bless him and give him peace."
sentences.n: ياسيدي is printed as one word: yā sayyidī, 'O my master'. The girl returns his greeting in full, with the fuller formula 'and God's mercy and blessings', as the Prophet's custom requires that a greeting be answered with an equal or better one.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا قَوْلُكَ كَيْفَ حَالُكَ فَإِنْ شِئْتَ أَنْ تَعْرِفَهُ فَلَا تَتَمَنَّاهُ إِلَّا لِأَعْدَائِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā qawluka kayfa ḥāluka fa-in shiʾta an taʿrifahu fa-lā tatamannāhu illā li-aʿdāʾika
sentences.l: And-as-for your-saying, how your-state, then-if you-wished that you-know-it, then-not you-wish-it except for-your-enemies.
sentences.i: As for your question, "How are you?", if you wish to know it, then wish it on none but your enemies.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَكَتَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma sakatat
sentences.l: Then she-fell-silent.
sentences.i: Then she fell silent.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ كَلَامَهَا طَارَ عَقْلُهُ فَرَحًا بِهَا ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْبَدَوِيِّ وَقَالَ لَهُ كَمْ ثَمَنُهَا فَإِنَّهَا جَلِيلَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru kalāmahā ṭāra ʿaqluhu faraḥan bihā thumma iltafata ilā al-badawiyyi wa-qāla lahu kam thamanuhā fa-innahā jalīlatun
sentences.l: And-when the-merchant heard her-speech, his-mind flew in-joy with-her; then he-turned to the-Bedouin and-said to-him: how-much her-price? for-indeed-she exalted.
sentences.i: When the merchant heard her words, his wits flew away for joy in her. Then he turned to the Bedouin and said: "What is her price? For she is a woman of high worth."
sentences.n: طَارَ عَقْلُهُ فَرَحًا, 'his mind flew with joy', is the Arabic idiom for being overjoyed. جَلِيلَة is 'great, exalted, of high worth'; the Bedouin takes the word as praise that will raise her price, and it angers him.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَاظَ الْبَدَوِيُّ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَفْسَدْتَ عَلَيَّ الْجَارِيَةَ بِهَذَا الْكَلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-ightāẓa al-badawiyyu wa-qāla lahu afsadta ʿalayya al-jāriyata bi-hādhā al-kalāmi
sentences.l: So-he-was-enraged the-Bedouin and-said to-him: you-spoiled upon-me the-girl with-this the-speech.
sentences.i: The Bedouin was enraged and said to him: "You have ruined the girl for me with this talk."
sentences.n: عَلَيَّ carries the shadda the print gives it. أَفْسَدْتَ عَلَيَّ means 'you have spoiled [her] to my harm', a dative of disadvantage.

sentences.t: لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ تَقُولُ أَنَّهَا جَلِيلَةٌ مَعَ أَنَّهَا مِنْ قُطَاعَةِ الْجَوَارِي وَرَعَاعِ النَّاسِ وَلَا أَبِيعُهَا لَكَ
sentences.tr: li-ayyi shayʾin taqūlu annahā jalīlatun maʿa annahā min quṭāʿati al-jawārī wa-raʿāʿi al-nāsi wa-lā abīʿuhā laka
sentences.l: For-which thing you-say that-she exalted, together-with that-she from the-scraps of-the-girls and-the-rabble of-the-people? And-not I-sell-her to-you.
sentences.i: "Why do you say she is of high worth, when she is of the dregs of slave-girls and the riff-raff of the people? And I will not sell her to you."
sentences.n: قُطَاعَة is read as 'what is cut off, scraps, leavings'; a lexical sense of the unpointed word that fits the insult, though قَطَّاعَة is conceivable. The last clause is the angry refusal of a man who has been told his goods are worth more than he thought.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ كَلَامَهُ عَرَفَ أَنَّهُ قَلِيلُ الْعَقْلِ وَقَالَ لَهُ رَيِّضْ خُلُقَكَ فَأَنَا أَشْتَرِيهَا عَلَى هَذِهِ الْعُيُوبِ الَّتِي ذَكَرْتَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru kalāmahu ʿarafa annahu qalīlu al-ʿaqli wa-qāla lahu rayyiḍ khuluqaka fa-anā ashtarīhā ʿalā hādhihi al-ʿuyūbi allatī dhakartahā
sentences.l: And-when the-merchant heard his-speech he-knew that-he few-of the-mind, and-said to-him: tame your-temper, for-I I-buy-her upon these the-faults which you-mentioned.
sentences.i: When the merchant heard what he said, he knew him to be a man of little sense, and said to him: "Curb your temper. I will buy her with all the faults you have named."
sentences.n: رَيِّضْ is the print's own marked word (ريّض): imperative of رَيَّضَ, 'to break in, tame' (as a colt); خُلُقَكَ is 'your temper, disposition'. عَلَى هَذِهِ الْعُيُوبِ means 'on the footing of these faults', that is, accepting her as described.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ وَكَمْ تَدْفَعُ لِي فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu wa-kam tadfaʿu lī fīhā
sentences.l: So-said the-Bedouin: and-how-much you-pay to-me in-her?
sentences.i: The Bedouin said: "And how much will you pay me for her?"

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ التَّاجِرُ مَايُسَمِّي الْوَلَدَ إِلَّا أَبُوهُ فَاطْلُبْ فِيهَا غَرَضَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-tājiru mā yusammī al-walada illā abūhu fa-uṭlub fīhā gharaḍaka
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-merchant: not he-names the-child except his-father; so-ask in-her your-aim.
sentences.i: The merchant said to him: "None names the child but its father; so name your own price for her."
sentences.n: مايسمي is printed as one word: mā yusammī, 'he does not name'. The proverb is turned to say that the seller, like a father, is the one to name the price. غَرَض is 'aim, object'; فِيهَا is 'for her'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ مَا يَتَكَلَّمُ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-badawiyyu mā yatakallamu illā anta
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-Bedouin: not he-speaks except you.
sentences.i: The Bedouin said to him: "It is you who must speak."
sentences.n: The speech is not finished here; it continues in the next unit. The sense is 'let no one speak but you', handing the merchant the first offer.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُ فِي نَفْسِهِ هَذَا الْبَدَوِيُّ مُقَرْقِعٌ نَاشِفُ الرَّأْسِ وَاللَّهِ أَنَالَا أَعْرِفُ لَهَا قِيمَةً إِلَّا أَنَّهَا مَلَكَتْ قَلْبِي بِفَصَاحَتِهَا وَحُسْنِ مَنْظَرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-tājiru fī nafsihi hādhā al-badawiyyu muqarqiʿun nāshifu al-raʾsi wa-allāhi anā lā aʿrifu lahā qīmatan illā annahā malakat qalbī bi-faṣāḥatihā wa-ḥusni manẓarihā
sentences.l: And the merchant said in himself: This Bedouin is a rattler, dry-of the head; by God, I-do-not know for her a value, except that she has taken-possession-of my heart by her eloquence and the beauty-of her look,
sentences.i: The merchant said to himself, “This Bedouin is a blustering blockhead. By God, I cannot put a price on her; I know only that she has taken my heart captive by her eloquence and her lovely looks,
sentences.n: أَنَالَا is two words run together in the print, أَنَا لَا, “I … not”: read it anā lā. مُقَرْقِعٌ is uncertain; it comes from qarqaʿa, “to rattle, clatter”, so “a rattler, a blusterer”, and ناشف الرأس “dry of head” is the colloquial for thick-skulled and stubborn; together they make a Bedouin who is all noise and no sense.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ كَانَتْ تَكْتُبُ وَتَقْرَأُ فَهَذَا مِنْ تَمَامِ النِّعْمَةِ عَلَيْهَا وَعَلَى مَنْ يَشْتَرِيهَا
sentences.tr: wa-in kānat taktubu wa-taqraʾu fa-hādhā min tamāmi al-niʿmati ʿalayhā wa-ʿalā man yashtarīhā
sentences.l: and if she was writing and reading, then this is of the completeness-of the favour upon her and upon him-who buys-her.
sentences.i: and if she can also write and read, that is the crowning of her blessing, both for her and for whoever buys her.

sentences.t: لَكِنْ هَذَا الْبَدَوِيُّ لَايَعْرِفُ لَهَا قِيمَةً
sentences.tr: lākin hādhā al-badawiyyu lā yaʿrifu lahā qīmatan
sentences.l: But this Bedouin, he-does-not-know for her a value.
sentences.i: But this Bedouin has no notion what she is worth.
sentences.n: لَايَعْرِفُ is لَا يَعْرِفُ run together in the print: lā yaʿrifu, “he does not know”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْبَدَوِيِّ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا شَيْخَ الْعَرَبِ أَدْفَعُ لَكَ فِيهَا مِائَتَيْ دِينَارٍ سَالِمَةً لِيَدِكَ خَارِجًا عَنِ الضَّمَانِ وَحَقِّ السُّلْطَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilā al-badawiyyi wa-qāla lahu yā shaykha al-ʿarabi adfaʿu laka fīhā miʾatay dīnārin sālimatan li-yadika khārijan ʿani al-ḍamāni wa-ḥaqqi al-sulṭāni
sentences.l: Then he-turned to the Bedouin and said to-him: O sheikh-of the Arabs, I-will-pay to-you for-her two-hundred-of dinars, sound into-your-hand, outside-of the surety and the due-of the Sultan.
sentences.i: Then he turned to the Bedouin and said, “Sheikh of the Arabs, I will pay you two hundred dinars for her, whole and clear into your own hand, free of the guarantee and the Sultan’s due.”
sentences.n: الضَّمَانِ is the surety or liability on the sale, and حَقّ السُّلْطَان the Sultan’s due, that is, any duty or levy; the merchant is offering a net sum with nothing deducted. The print spells “two hundred” مائتي with the hamza on a ya, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ ذَلِكَ الْبَدَوِيُّ اِغْتَاظَ عَيْظًا شَدِيدًا وَصَرَخَ عَلَى التَّاجِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa dhālika al-badawiyyu ightāẓa ʿayẓan shadīdan wa-ṣarakha ʿalā al-tājiri
sentences.l: And when he-heard that, the Bedouin, he-was-enraged a-rage intense, and he-shouted upon the merchant
sentences.i: When the Bedouin heard this, he flew into a violent rage and shouted at the merchant,
sentences.n: عَيْظًا is a print slip for غَيْظًا (ghayẓan), “rage”, kept as printed; read it ghayẓan. The cognate accusative (“enraged a rage”) is ordinary Arabic emphasis.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ قُمْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِكَ وَاللَّهِ إِنْ أَعْطَيْتَنِي مِائَتَيْ دِينَارٍ فِي هَذِهِ الْقِطْعَةِ الْعَبَاءَةِ الَّتِي عَلَيْهَا مَا بِعْتُهَا لَكَ وَأَنَا مَا عُدْتُ أَبِيعُهَا بَلْ أُخَلِّيهَا عِنْدِي تَرْعَيٰ الْجِمَالَ وَتَطْحَنُ الطَّحِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu qum ilā ḥāli sabīlika wa-allāhi in aʿṭaytanī miʾatay dīnārin fī hādhihi al-qiṭʿati al-ʿabāʾati allatī ʿalayhā mā biʿtuhā laka wa-anā mā ʿudtu abīʿuhā bal ukhallīhā ʿindī tarʿā al-jimāla wa-taṭḥanu al-ṭaḥīna
sentences.l: and said to-him: Rise to the state-of your-way! By God, if you-gave-me two-hundred-of dinars for this piece, the cloak that is upon her, I-did-not-sell-her to-you; and I, I-have-not returned selling-her, rather I-leave-her with-me, she-pastures the camels and grinds the flour.
sentences.i: and said, “Be gone about your business! By God, if you gave me two hundred dinars for this very cloak she is wearing, I still would not sell her to you. I have given up selling her; I shall keep her by me to tend the camels and grind the flour.”
sentences.n: قُمْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِكَ, “get up to the state of your road”, is a dismissal: go your way. In ما بعتها لك the perfect after the oath and the condition means “I would not have sold her”. ما عدت ابيعها is “I no longer sell her”. تَرْعَيٰ is printed with a ya for the final alif of ترعى, and carries the dagger alif; read tarʿā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَاحَ عَلَيْهَا وَقَالَ تَعَالِي يَامُنْتِنَةُ أَنَالَا أَبِيعُكِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣāḥa ʿalayhā wa-qāla taʿālī yā muntinatu anā lā abīʿuki
sentences.l: Then he-cried-out upon her and said: Come, O stinking-one! I-do-not sell-you.
sentences.i: Then he bawled at her, “Come here, you stinking creature! I am not selling you.”
sentences.n: يَامُنْتِنَةُ is يَا مُنْتِنَةُ run together in the print, “O foul-smelling one”, and أَنَالَا is أَنَا لَا, “I … not”. تَعَالِي is the feminine imperative: he is speaking to the girl.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى التَّاجِرِ وَقَالَ لَهُ كُنْتُ أَحْسِبُكَ أَهْلَ مَعْرِفَةٍ وَحَقِّ طُرْطُورِي إِنْ لَمْ تَذْهَبْ عَنِّي لَأُسْمِعَنَّكَ مَا لَا يُرْضِيكَ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilā al-tājiri wa-qāla lahu kuntu aḥsibuka ahla maʿrifatin wa-ḥaqqi ṭurṭūrī in lam tadhhab ʿannī la-usmiʿannaka mā lā yurḍīka
sentences.l: Then he-turned to the merchant and said to-him: I-was reckoning-you a-man-of knowledge; and by-the-right-of my ṭurṭūr-cap, if you-do-not-go from-me, I-will-surely-make-you-hear what does-not please-you.
sentences.i: Then he turned to the merchant and said, “I took you for a man of discernment. By my cap, if you do not take yourself off, I shall make you hear what will not please you!”
sentences.n: طُرْطُور is the tall pointed cap; swearing by one’s cap is a plainly comic Bedouin oath, and the merchant seizes on it in the next sentence as proof of madness. In لَاُسْمِعَنَّكَ the lam is the emphatic “surely” of an oath-threat and the ending -nna the emphatic of the verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّ هَذَا الْبَدَوِيَّ مَجْنُونٌ وَلَا يَعْرِفُ قِيمَتَهَا وَلَا أَقُولُ لَهُ شَيْأً فِي ثَمَنِهَا فِى هَذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-tājiru fī nafsihi inna hādhā al-badawiyya majnūnun wa-lā yaʿrifu qīmatahā wa-lā aqūlu lahu shayʾan fī thamanihā fī hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: And the merchant said in himself: Indeed this Bedouin is mad, and he-does-not-know her value, and I-do-not-say to-him anything about her price at this time,
sentences.i: The merchant said to himself, “This Bedouin is mad; he has no notion of her worth, and I shall say nothing to him about her price just now,
sentences.n: The print spells the second فِى with a dotless ya (فى هذا); read fī. شيأ is the print’s spelling of شيء, “thing”.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ صَاحِبَ عَقْلٍ مَا قَالَ وَحَقِّ طُرْطُورِي وَاللَّهِ إِنَّهَا تُسَاوِي مُلْكَ كِسْرَى وَأَنَا مَا مَعِي ثَمَنُهَا وَلَكِنْ إِنْ طَلَبَ مِنِّي زِيَادَةً أُعْطِيهِ مَا يُرِيدُ وَلَوْ أَخَذَ جَمِيعَ مَا لِي
sentences.tr: fa-innahu law kāna ṣāḥiba ʿaqlin mā qāla wa-ḥaqqi ṭurṭūrī wa-allāhi innahā tusāwī mulka kisrā wa-anā mā maʿī thamanuhā wa-lākin in ṭalaba minnī ziyādatan uʿṭīhi mā yurīdu wa-law akhadha jamīʿa mā lī
sentences.l: for indeed-he, if he-were possessor-of reason he-would-not-have-said “by-the-right-of my ṭurṭūr-cap”; and by God, indeed-she equals the-kingdom-of Khosrow, and I, not with-me her price; but if he-asks of-me an-increase, I-give-him what he-wants, even if he-take all-of what is-to-me.
sentences.i: for if he had any sense he would not have said “by my cap”. By God, she is worth the kingdom of Khosrow, and I do not have her price about me; but if he asks more of me, I shall give him whatever he wants, though he take everything I own.”
sentences.n: كِسْرَى is Khosrow, the Persian king, as a figure for boundless wealth. مَا لِي, “what is to me”, is the ordinary way of saying “all that I own”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْبَدَوِيِّ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا شَيْخَ الْعَرَبِ طَوِّلْ بَالَكَ وَرَيِّضْ نَفْسَكَ وَقُلْ لِي مَا لَهَا مِنَ الْقُمَاشِ عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilā al-badawiyyi wa-qāla lahu yā shaykha al-ʿarabi ṭawwil bālaka wa-rayyiḍ nafsaka wa-qul lī mā lahā mina al-qumāshi ʿindaka
sentences.l: Then he-turned to the Bedouin and said to-him: O sheikh-of the Arabs, lengthen your-mind and tame your-self, and say to-me what is-for-her of the cloth with-you.
sentences.i: Then he turned to the Bedouin and said, “Sheikh of the Arabs, be patient and compose yourself, and tell me what clothing she has with you.”
sentences.n: طَوِّلْ بَالَكَ, “lengthen your mind”, is the idiom for “be patient”. The print marks both طوّل and ريّض with a shadda, which we keep. رَيِّضْ is probably the form of رَوَّضَ / رَاضَ, “to break in, tame”, with the middle waw written as ya; the sense is “calm yourself”. The merchant’s question is what garments the girl has on or with her; the Bedouin takes it as a question of what suits her.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ وَمَا يَصْلُحُ لِهَذِهِ الْكُورَةِ مِنَ الْقُمَاشِ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ هَذِهِ الْعَبَاءَةَ الَّتِي هِيَ مَلْفُوفَةٌ فِيهَا كَثِيرَةٌ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-badawiyyu wa-mā yaṣluḥu li-hādhihi al-kūrati mina al-qumāshi wa-allāhi inna hādhihi al-ʿabāʾata allatī hiya malfūfatun fīhā kathīratun ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And he-said to-him, the Bedouin: And what is-fitting for-this kūra of the cloth? By God, indeed this cloak that she is wrapped in it is too-much upon-her.
sentences.i: The Bedouin answered, “What cloth is fit for a lump like this? By God, the cloak she is wrapped in is more than she deserves.”
sentences.n: الْكُورَةِ is obscure. In the lexica kūra is a district or province, which makes no sense said of a girl; the colloquial sense may be “a lump, a clod”, a contemptuous word for her, and that is how we have taken it. كَثِيرَةٌ عَلَيْهَا, “much upon her”, is the colloquial “too much for her”. Note the resumptive pronoun in الَّتِي هِيَ مَلْفُوفَةٌ فِيهَا, “which she is wrapped in it”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ التَّاجِرُ عَنْ إِذْنِكَ أَكْشِفُ عَنْ وَجْهِهَا وَأَقْلِبُهَا كَمَا يُقَلِّبُ النَّاسُ الْجَوَارِيَ لِأَجْلِ الِاشْتِرَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-tājiru ʿan idhnika akshifu ʿan wajhihā wa-aqlibuhā kamā yuqallibu al-nāsu al-jawāriya li-ajli al-ishtirāʾi
sentences.l: And he-said to-him, the merchant: From your-permission I-uncover from her face and I-turn-her, as the people turn-over the slave-girls for-the-sake-of the buying.
sentences.i: The merchant said, “With your leave, let me uncover her face and turn her about, as people examine slave-girls when they mean to buy.”
sentences.n: عَنْ إِذْنِكَ is “with your leave”. The two verbs أَكْشِفُ and أَقْلِبُهَا stand in the plain indicative where Classical Arabic would use a subjunctive after a request: this is the Middle Arabic way of saying “let me”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ دُونَكَ وَمَا تُرِيدُ اللَّهُ يَحْفَظُ شَبَابَكَ فَقَلِّبْهَا ظَاهِرًا وَبَاطِنًا وَإِنْ شِئْتَ فَعَرِّهَا الثِّيَابَ ثُمَّ اُنْظُرْهَا وَهِيَ عُرْيَانَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-badawiyyu dūnaka wa-mā turīdu allāhu yaḥfaẓu shabābaka fa-qallibhā ẓāhiran wa-bāṭinan wa-in shiʾta fa-ʿarrihā al-thiyāba thumma unẓurhā wa-hiya ʿuryānatun
sentences.l: And he-said to-him, the Bedouin: Here-you-are and what you-want! God preserves your-youth! So turn-her outside and inside, and if you-wish, strip-her the-clothes, then look-at-her while-she naked.
sentences.i: “She is yours, and do as you please,” said the Bedouin. “God keep your youth! Turn her over, inside and out; and if you wish, strip her of her clothes and look at her naked.”
sentences.n: دُونَكَ, “(take) what is below you”, is the stock “here you are, help yourself”. اللَّهُ يَحْفَظُ شَبَابَكَ is a courtesy formula, “God keep your youth”. The print marks فعرّها with a shadda, which we keep: ʿarrihā is “strip her”, with the clothes as a second object.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُ مَعَاذَ اللَّهِ أَنَا مَا أَنْظُرُ إِلَّا وَجْهَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-tājiru maʿādha allāhi anā mā anẓuru illā wajhahā
sentences.l: And he-said, the merchant: Refuge-of God! I, I-do-not look except her face.
sentences.i: “God forbid!” said the merchant. “I shall look at nothing but her face.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ التَّاجِرَ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهَا وَهُوَ خَجْلَانُ مِنْ حُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-tājira taqaddama ilayhā wa-huwa khajlānu min ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā
sentences.l: Then indeed the merchant advanced to-her, and he bashful from her beauty and her comeliness,
sentences.i: Then the merchant stepped up to her, abashed by her beauty and her grace,

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُ—بَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mu—bāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The print splits the last word with a dash, الم—باح, and we keep it as printed; read al-mubāḥ. The whole is the stock closing formula of a night: the morning overtakes Shahrazād, and she stops speaking “the permitted speech”, that is, the story she was allowed to tell. Her name is printed as two words, شهر زاد.
